Alright, so this vLog update is going to be a bit more technical then the last, since I'm using this as more of a brain dump then an actual vLog post. It's going to help me work through a couple of things:

  • How the fuck Minecraft colorizes grass and foliage
  • How the fuck LibGDX renders Tiled maps so I can tear it apart and modify it to colorize my grass and foliage in Tranquility
  • All the failed attempts at trying to colorize things, and what I learned to try for the next time.

So, let's begin at the beginning: How the Minecraft Colorizer works (at least know I currently have it figured out).

After downloading FML and poking through the render code a bit, I found the LayeredColorMaskTexture class in /net/minecraft/client/renderer/texture. From what I can tell, it's responsible for loading the colormask that the foliage and grass uses. Since LibGDX manages loading resources, I don't need that code, but it set me in the right area to start looking for ties to that class name.

Next came the BlockGrass class in /net/minecraft/block. It had the helper functions getBlockColor(), getRenderColor(IBlockState state), and colorMultiplier(IBlockAccess worldIn, BlockPos pos, int renderPass). The getRenderColor() function returned getBlockColor(), so I can ignore that. The getBlockColor() returned a value from a helper class called ColorizerGrass, specifically ColorizerGrass.getGrassColor(0.5D, 1.0D). The mouseover hint says the two args, in order, are temp and humidity. This is, more or less, the code I'm looking for to pull a value from the ColorMask and layer it over a grayscale.

The ColorizerGrass class has two functions, setGrassBiomeColorizer(int[] grassBuffer) and getGrassColor(double temp, double humidity). The setGrassBiomeColorizer() sets the grassBuffer array, which is 65536 ints big (That number gets thrown around a lot in minecraft, not sure why, it's not the max value of any of the primitives Java has, either signed or unsigned). The getGrassColor() function is interesting though:

It first multiplies the humidity variable by the temp variable (both the original passed in variables) and saves it in the humidity variable (again, the same one that was passed in).
It then subtracts 1.0D from the passed in temp variable, then times that by 255.0D, then casts that into an integer to be stored in a local variable.
It does the same thing with the humidity variable that was passed in.
It then takes the local variable for humidity, bitshifts it left by 8, then bitwise OR's it by the local temp variable, and stores it in it's own local variable.
Finally, it returns either -65281 (if the voodoo magic local variable from above is greater than the length of the grassBuffer) or the number in the grassBuffer array that's at where-ever the voodoo magic local variable number is at.

In code, it looks like this:

argHumidity *= argTemp; 
int localTemp = (int)((1.0D-argTemp)*255.0D); 
int localHumidity = (int)((1.0D-argHumidity)*255.0D); 
int voodoo = localHumidity << 8 | localTemp; 
return voodoo > grassBuffer.length ? -65281 : grassBuffer[voodoo];

So now I got part of the codewise implementation (how it picks colors based on temp and humidity), So I have to figure out how I want to modify it to work within what I want for Tranquility.

Tranquility is going to have weather (like Harvest Moon 64, with the rain and snow and the storms that would fuck your shit up) and it's going to come with all the weather-related things, like precipitation and such. The temperature is going to be set based on what time of season it is (much like how most Harvest Moon games do it, with Spring, Summer, Fall, and Winter instead of using the 12 month system like Animal Crossing). I believe I can get this code working with minimal modifications from how Minecraft does it (without, you know, directly copying it because that's bad #ThanksOracle).

This also rasies another issue that I'm going to look into when I take that step: is there a way to get a single Tile on the map? I assume there is, it would be stupid if there wasn't, but might as well write it down so I don't forget it.

Now that I got about half of the code that I needed to find found, it's time to look into what colorMultiplier() does, because that might help with figuring out where the grassBuffer is set in ColorizerGrass.

So colorMultiplier returns an int that BiomeColorHelper.getGrassColorAtPos(IBlockAccess worldIn, BlockPos pos) returns, so that's the next stop on this wild ride that is the partial Minecraft source code.

And that's where this ride gets fun. A good chunk of this code is still vastly obfusicated with the lack of human-readable names, so it'll take quite a bit of time to figure out what the fuck is going on. And it's going to be something I'm not going to touch right now, since I don't have the required amount of liqour in me to do something like that. So, on to figuring out where ColorizerGrass.setGrassBiomeColorizer() is called. Hopefully that doesn't require liqour.

A quick recursive grep brings up only one hit, GrassColorReloadListener. The grassBuffer is actually the raw image data from the grass colormask. Before I actually look at it, I'm assuming that the array is literally just the colors in that image stored in an int.

And I was right. It's using an AWT BufferedImage and the BufferedImage.getRGB() to store it in an int array that is height times width big (assuming somewhere near 65536). Alright, neat. I wonder if LibGDX's image helper classes have something like that, or if I'm going to have to do it this way. I'm going to have to look later.

Since now I know what the array is made of, I would like to know how the values it holds are reconstructed. I assuming a whole bunch of bit shifting and voodoo magic.

And that's where the trail turns cold. Other then the classes that implement getBlockColor(), there are no other mentions or it in the code when I grep for it, so I assume that either

  • FML doesn't have a full deobf of the minecraft source, which is really likely, or
  • I'm a moron, which is just as likely.

However, thanks to my uber elite skills at life (aka Google and GrepCode), I found the official Oracle implementation of BufferedImage.getRGB(). I can use that to figure out how the int is encoded, and with any luck, be able to decode it back into the RGB colorspace.

So what I can gather, the int in encoded like so:

0Xxx000000 is the alpha value 
0X00xx0000 is red 
0X0000xx00 is green 
0X000000xx is blue

So shifting the bits needed would be able to pull out the values needed per color between 0 and 255, which is awesome because most every implementation of color in anything uses those numbers for color values per channel.

So now, my goal would be to use this knowledge and start hacking away. I'm more then likely going to write up another brain dump soonish when I start working on heavily modifying the TiledRenderer that LibGDX has so I can abuse it to do as I want.

At first glance, The Babadook may sound like a tale that warns people to not let children put creepy stories up into their heads. It may also be like one of those old horror movies with children being influenced by the ghost. The titular monster seems to have the potential of being a silly urban legend, such as Slender Man or the Hash Slinging Slasher (sorry about that), that is destined to be flooded with fan fiction, or simply just another horror movie icon, but the film surprisingly has a different aim than just scaring the audience. It might as well be a character study of a mother having a hard time moving on after the tragedy she's been through losing her husband and trying to raise her only son. The real horror doesn't come out that quick, but there is already a pretty compelling movie when it come to its characters. The tension is just the prize for being intrigued by the story's core.

One thing people must know about the film is it's not generally about The Babadook monster. In spite that the antagonist has an ambitiously great campy design and his story is told well by a twisted storybook with wondrously illustrated diorama, the movie is still laden on the more human element of the tale, which is the struggle of a mother who is unable to live normally. The pacing of her life may move too fast for the film, but the sadness and deprivation beneath those regular troubling days are totally manifested even without extending any of its breathing. The plot mostly concerns Amelia finding a way to overcome Samuel's behavioral issues and her memories with the accident than dealing with the whole supernatural threat, for sure it is trying to build some slow burn, but even without that horror movie sense, it still feels like they're being tormented by life.

It deliberately takes their personal grief seriously, making sure that they actually aren't insane, and nobody else could ever understand what they're going through. This is pretty much the most compelling view of the film, which makes them reasonably trapped into their own nightmares. Mister Babadook only becomes the boiling point of the ordeal. And when it hits to the part of the real scares, it sells well whenever the monster attacks. Instead of loud lazy jump scares, it rather spreads away signs of his presence and its effects to the family. His appearance has more terror if he's lurking in the shadows. It also has a nice use of practical effects to endure its very effective creeps. The performances of the two leads are outstanding for bringing the real heart of the picture. Essie Davis embraces the character, making her fear, depression, and shifting madness all visibly genuine. Same to the young Noah Wiseman who as well gives his character's actions some sense of anxiety.

Some horror fans might get slightly disappointed for not giving The Babadook monster enough of the characterization he deserves. The other story is a lot more interesting to follow than his diorama tricks, and that is why I keep stating that the the movie is best viewed as a gloomy fairytale about a mother and a son fighting to keep a hold of themselves and promise to protect each other from the odds, even if the promise doesn't always apply, than just another horror movie being shown in our theaters. While it still has the right amount of admirably campy scares, the film often explores to the larger and much affecting side of the story, and that sure offers beyond than what you expect to this stale genre.
